What does this test show about the hypothesis? supported: every check HELD and the test was a fair one. refuted: a check FAILED and the test was a fair one. inconclusive: the test was not fair (name the defect and what a fair test would compare), or the checks disagree. A check that failed because another setting limited the result, or one that held although it would have held under a rival explanation too, is not a fair test. The defects: none: no defect; not_about_the_guess: the hypothesis would come out the same whether the guess is true or not, or is about another cause than the guess; rival_passes_too: a rival explanation predicts the same outcome of the decision rule, so the test cannot tell the two apart; already_answered: the very value this test asks for already stands in the ledger or in a tool's result: read it there instead of testing for it; confounded: another setting, at the values chosen, limits or hides the effect, so the result would not show what the hypothesis says; threshold: the rule's threshold or margin makes it hold or fail whatever happens, or lies inside the tolerance.

The guess of why: The scheduler gives TCP a separate service share, so TCP data and ACKs survive; the earlier near-zero TCP result was caused by shared FIFO tail-drop under UDP overload, not by the TCP controller.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: TCP likely never establishes; the three retransmissions are SYN retransmissions dropped by the full FIFO queue, so no ACKs or data are measured.
  [Y2] guess: Queue length controls whether TCP's handshake can occur before the queue becomes persistently full; a much larger queue may let TCP connect.
  [Y3] guess: Once TCP is connected, FIFO tail-drop with UDP excess imposes very high loss on TCP; a loss-insensitive controller such as BBR may retain more throughput than Cubic.
  [Y4] guess: TCP can put segments in flight but almost no ACK clock survives; the limiter is FIFO tail-drop under UDP overload, not the congestion-control algorithm's loss response.
  [Y5] guess: A larger FIFO queue only lets a few handshake/data packets through before persistent saturation; the queue discipline remains the main limiter.
  [Y6] guess: Lost TCP segments cause RTO stalls far longer than queue wait, so delivery occurs only in rare successful windows rather than in steady congestion control.
  [H1] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, tcp_goodput_bps is greater than 0 because the handshake can complete before saturation.
  [H2] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, l1_util_back is greater than 0 because an established TCP flow produces ACKs.
  [H3] hypothesis (refuted): At l1.queue.length=1000, TcpBbr gives higher tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic because BBR does not collapse on the UDP-induced loss.
  [H4] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 by a scheduler makes tcp_goodput_bps exceed 100 Mbps.

The result it starts from, as the researcher states it: Under the scheduler, TCP gets 476482765 bps and UDP gets 489424320 bps, together about 965.9 Mbps of the 1 Gbps link.
The guess of why: The scheduler allocates roughly equal bandwidth to the two backlogged flows, so TCP's ceiling under this UDP load is about half the link.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: TCP likely never establishes; the three retransmissions are SYN retransmissions dropped by the full FIFO queue, so no ACKs or data are measured.
  [Y2] guess: Queue length controls whether TCP's handshake can occur before the queue becomes persistently full; a much larger queue may let TCP connect.
  [Y3] guess: Once TCP is connected, FIFO tail-drop with UDP excess imposes very high loss on TCP; a loss-insensitive controller such as BBR may retain more throughput than Cubic.
  [Y4] guess: TCP can put segments in flight but almost no ACK clock survives; the limiter is FIFO tail-drop under UDP overload, not the congestion-control algorithm's loss response.
  [Y5] guess: A larger FIFO queue only lets a few handshake/data packets through before persistent saturation; the queue discipline remains the main limiter.
  [Y6] guess: Lost TCP segments cause RTO stalls far longer than queue wait, so delivery occurs only in rare successful windows rather than in steady congestion control.
  [H1] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, tcp_goodput_bps is greater than 0 because the handshake can complete before saturation.
  [H2] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, l1_util_back is greater than 0 because an established TCP flow produces ACKs.
  [H3] hypothesis (refuted): At l1.queue.length=1000, TcpBbr gives higher tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic because BBR does not collapse on the UDP-induced loss.
  [H4] hypothesis (inconclusive): With l1.queue.length=1000 and TcpCubic, replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 by a scheduler makes tcp_goodput_bps exceed 100 Mbps.

THE RULINGS SO FAR:
  [V1] on H1: inconclusive. C1 held because r002 tcp_goodput_bps=5792 exceeds r001 tcp_goodput_bps=0, but that only shows q1000_cubic gives some TCP goodput, not that the handshake completed before saturation. A rival explanation, such as the larger queue letting TCP connect or get a small share after saturation, predicts the same 5792 > 0 result, so the test cannot tell the guess apart.
  [V2] on H2: inconclusive. The failed check is not a fair refutation because l1_util_back=0.0 in r002 while tcp_goodput_bps=5792, so the metric did not reveal the ACK traffic the hypothesis expects. A fair test would compare an established-TCP indicator such as tcp_goodput_bps or ACK-related counters, not l1_util_back alone.
  [V3] on H3: refuted. The fair check failed: in r002 TcpCubic at l1.queue.length=1000 has tcp_goodput_bps=5792, while in r003 TcpBbr has tcp_goodput_bps=4634, so 4634 is not greater than 1.01*5792. THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpCubic, TcpNewReno, TcpLinuxReno, TcpBbr, TcpVegas, TcpBic, default TcpCubic)
TOLERANCE: two results that differ by less than 1 % count as equal.

THE RESULT the guess is about: T27/T29 show r004 sched Cubic tcp_inflight mean 1048576 bytes at tcp_rtt_ms mean 17.217 ms (1048576*8/0.017217 = 487.6 Mbps, matching its 476482765 bps goodput) with its queue nonempty for all 10.1 s (T31), while T28/T30 show r005 sched BBR inflight 6790 bytes at 0.218 ms RTT.
THE GUESS of why it came out so: Cubic's own ~950-packet scheduler queue inflates its RTT to 17 ms while its inflight is pinned near 1 MiB, so it delivers inflight/RTT just under the scheduler's ~50% share; shortening the queue cuts that self-inflicted RTT and should lift TCP toward the share, whereas BBR's low share comes from its small inflight, not from RTT.
THE HYPOTHESIS H9: With the sender-side scheduler and TcpCubic, l1.queue.length=500 gives tcp_goodput_bps more than 1% above the l1.queue.length=1000 value of 476482765 bps.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: TCP likely never establishes; the three retransmissions are SYN retransmissions dropped by the full FIFO queue, so no ACKs or data are measured.
  [Y2] guess: Queue length controls whether TCP's handshake can occur before the queue becomes persistently full; a much larger queue may let TCP connect.
  [Y3] guess: Once TCP is connected, FIFO tail-drop with UDP excess imposes very high loss on TCP; a loss-insensitive controller such as BBR may retain more throughput than Cubic.
  [Y4] guess: TCP can put segments in flight but almost no ACK clock survives; the limiter is FIFO tail-drop under UDP overload, not the congestion-control algorithm's loss response.
  [Y5] guess: A larger FIFO queue only lets a few handshake/data packets through before persistent saturation; the queue discipline remains the main limiter.
  [Y6] guess: Lost TCP segments cause RTO stalls far longer than queue wait, so delivery occurs only in rare successful windows rather than in steady congestion control.
  [Y7] guess: The scheduler allocates roughly equal bandwidth to the two backlogged flows, so TCP's ceiling under this UDP load is about half the link.
  [Y8] guess: If the scheduler is a per-flow fair-share queue, TCP congestion-control choice and l1.queue.length should have little effect on tcp_goodput_bps; if it is a priority or loss-sensitive queue, those settings should change TCP goodput.
  [Y9] guess: The scheduler serves nonempty per-flow queues, so TCP's share is set by whether its queue stays backlogged; Cubic fills its queue and gets about half the link, while BBR's lower inflight leaves its queue less backlogged and UDP takes the surplus.
